documents.unit: Office of the Provost (Joint University Curriculum Committee)
documents.title: Syllabus Statement Options for Generative AI
documents.stance_why: The page sets no single rule; it says "you may choose one of three options" (comprehensive use with attribution, use only within instructor parameters, or discouraged/not permitted unless stated) and calls them "templates that can be customized". Because it offers tiers and hands the decision to instructors, the stance is delegates.
tiers: Comprehensive use of generative AI permitted with appropriate attribution
Use permitted only within instructor-given parameters, specific to each assignment, with attribution
Use strongly discouraged or not permitted unless explicitly stated by the instructor
documents.summary: A provost-approved set of three customizable syllabus statements on generative AI, ranging from open use with attribution to discouragement or prohibition. The page also carries a note to instructors cautioning that bans may be unenforceable and raise equity problems, and records the committee and provost approvals.

units.why: The page says "you may choose one of three options", so the university gives instructors a menu of named AI-use levels rather than one rule. This is a tiers policy (P05), not just instructor choice (P04), because the options are fixed and ranked by permissiveness.
units.anchor: you may choose one of three options to address the use of generative AI tools

units.why: "These statements are templates that can be customized to fit your course context" lets each instructor adapt the wording, so the decision sits with the course. P04 fits because customization per course is the delegation; P110 (sample language) is also close but this sentence is about who decides.
units.anchor: These statements are templates that can be customized to fit your course context.

units.why: Option 1 states that "the comprehensive use of generative AI tools is permitted with appropriate attribution", an open-with-conditions default for courses that choose it. That is P02 (permit by default), with the attribution condition coded separately.
units.anchor: the comprehensive use of generative AI tools is permitted with appropriate attribution

units.why: Option 2 says use "is only permitted within the parameters provided by the instructor, specific to each assignment". The rule is set per assignment by the instructor, so P04 fits; P107 (closed list of tasks) does not because the list is not fixed in the document.
units.anchor: only permitted within the parameters provided by the instructor, specific to each assignment

units.why: Option 3 is "strongly discouraged or not permitted unless explicitly stated by the instructor", which sets what applies when the instructor has not allowed AI. It is a fallback of no use unless allowed (P06) rather than P03, because the text also allows outright prohibition.
units.anchor: strongly discouraged or not permitted unless explicitly stated by the instructor
units.frag_start: The use of generative AI tools
units.fit_note: The option also allows only 'strongly discouraged' wording, so it can be soft discouragement (P03) instead of a ban.

units.why: "Students must present work that is authentically their own" is a statement that submitted work must be the student's own, tied to the Honor Code. P29 (students own what they submit) fits directly.
units.anchor: students must present work that is authentically their own

units.why: Option 2 requires use to come "with appropriate attribution", so students must acknowledge AI use in the work. That is P24 (disclose with each submission); no tool, prompt or log details are required, so P25 and P26 do not apply.
units.anchor: specific to each assignment, with appropriate attribution
units.policy: Where generative AI use is permitted, it must be accompanied by appropriate attribution.

units.why: "Please ask your instructor to clarify any questions you may have" tells students who are unsure about a course's AI rule to ask the instructor. That is P10.
units.anchor: please ask your instructor to clarify any questions you may have

units.why: "This policy may be different from other course AI policies" warns that one course's AI permissions do not carry to another. That is P11; the sentence informs students and does not itself set a rule.
units.anchor: As this policy may be different from other course AI policies

units.why: "To mitigate risks associated with the use of generative AI, please review the Guidelines for Responsible Use" points students to a separate university guideline. P115 (point to further guidance) fits; the guideline's content is not in this text.
units.anchor: To mitigate risks associated with the use of generative AI, please review the
units.policy: Students review the Guidelines for Responsible Use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) at USF to mitigate risks associated with the use of generative AI.

units.why: "If the use of generative AI tools is permitted at any interval in the course, specific instructions must be followed" requires students to follow whatever instructions apply when AI is allowed in a discouraged-AI course. P78 (follow each course's rules) is nearest; the staging of 'any interval' also resembles P08 but nothing says permission grows over time.
units.anchor: permitted at any interval in the course, specific instructions must be followed.

units.why: The note tells instructors "Do not include both" 'strongly discouraged' and 'not permitted' "as this will be confusing to students". It is advice on wording the rule clearly, closest to P66 (word the rules with care), though P66 is about explaining rules to students.
units.anchor: Do not include both, as this will be confusing to students.
units.fit_note: The unit is about choosing one unambiguous wording for the statement, not explaining reasons or discussing AI with students.

units.why: The note says a ban "may not be enforceable" and that bans or unclear expectations drive "their use underground". That admits AI use cannot be fully prevented, which is P82.
units.anchor: it may not be enforceable
units.policy: Prohibiting GenAI tools use or not providing clear expectations drives their use underground, and the third syllabus statement may not be enforceable.

units.why: The note says driving use underground "presents a significant equity issue, privileging students who have more sophisticated language abilities and/or expertise with GenAI tools". This is an equity argument against bans. P51 is about cost and access, so I used UNCOVERED.
units.anchor: This presents a significant equity issue, privileging students who have more sophisticated language abilities
units.uncovered_note: Warns instructors that banning AI or leaving expectations unclear is an equity problem because it favors students with stronger language skills or AI expertise.

units.why: The note says GenAI "is increasingly embedded in a range of technologies" so students may not know when they are using it. It concerns AI inside other tools, which is P07; it is informational.
units.anchor: GenAI functionality, which is increasingly embedded in a range of technologies
units.fit_note: The unit does not set a rule on embedded AI; it only notes that students may not realize they are using it.

units.why: The note calls it "an important consideration in terms of punitive consequences" that students may not know they are using GenAI. That cautions instructors to be careful before penalizing, which is closest to P68 (respond educatively, not only punitively).
units.anchor: This is an important consideration in terms of punitive consequences.
units.fit_note: The unit only asks instructors to weigh the difficulty of telling when AI is used before punishing; it does not prescribe educative responses.

units.why: The page says the JUCC recommended the options and "the Provost approved the JUCC's recommendation". It states who made and approved the policy and when, which is P84.
units.anchor: the Provost approved the JUCC's recommendation
units.policy: The Joint University Curriculum Committee recommended the Syllabus Statement Options for Generative AI on May 16, 2024, and the Provost approved the recommendation on July 15, 2024.

units.why: The page records that in October 2025 the JUCC "recommended updates to the USF syllabus statements" and the Provost approved them. This shows the statements were revised, which is P54 (revisit regularly), although it records one revision and no cycle.
units.anchor: the JUCC recommended updates to the USF syllabus statements and customization guide
units.fit_note: The text records one past revision; it does not commit to regular review.

units.why: "The three statements are already embedded in your syllabus and ready to edit" in Simple Syllabus means the university supplies the template text in its syllabus tool. That is P110 (provide sample syllabus language).
units.anchor: the three statements are already embedded in your syllabus and ready to edit

units.why: Instructors are asked to "reference the Faculty Considerations for Syllabus Statement Customization before choosing a statement", which directs them to further guidance before they decide. P115 fits.
units.anchor: reference the Faculty Considerations for Syllabus Statement Customization before choosing a statement

documents.title: DLI Generative AI Hub
documents.stance_why: The hub says USF "welcomes innovation" while "cautiously and judiciously exploring" GenAI, and requires following existing technology policies, but it sets no rule on whether students may use AI in coursework; that is passed to syllabus statements. It is a hub of guidance, so the stance is delegates.
documents.summary: An ITS hub page defining generative AI, framing the risks of data security, compliance, copyright and academic integrity, and listing training, consultation and syllabus resources. It sets data-classification limits by tool type and requires technology assessment and the use of the university's responsible-use guidelines, which are not in the saved text.

units.why: The page defines GenAI as "a branch of artificial intelligence that specializes in creating new content", which sets what the guidance covers. That is P61.
units.anchor: GenAI is a branch of artificial intelligence that specializes in creating new content.

units.why: "USF welcomes innovation by exploring the exciting possibilities of GenAI tools" states a welcoming institutional posture. P02 (permit or encourage by default) is the nearest type, but the statement is about the university's exploration, not student use.
units.anchor: USF welcomes innovation by exploring the exciting possibilities of GenAI tools
units.fit_note: The welcome is directed at institutional exploration of GenAI tools, not a default rule for student use.

units.why: The page lists "information security and data privacy, compliance, copyright, and academic integrity" as the considerations when using these tools. It names the principles behind the guidance, so P56 (institution-wide framework) fits; the list is a preamble, not a rule.
units.anchor: information security and data privacy, compliance, copyright, and academic integrity

units.why: USF is "cautiously and judiciously exploring" GenAI because "ill-conceived and rushed deployments may introduce risks to data privacy and security". This sets the institution's guiding stance of cautious adoption, so P56 fits better than P118, which is about individuals weighing risks.
units.anchor: USF is cautiously and judiciously exploring Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI)

units.why: "You must follow the University's Technology Resources Appropriate Use Policy, Information Security Policy, and Guidelines for Responsible Use" binds anyone using GenAI to existing policies. That is P77.
units.anchor: you must follow the University's
units.frag_end: Use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) at USF
units.policy: Anyone considering using Generative AI tools must follow the University's Technology Resources Appropriate Use Policy, Information Security Policy, and Guidelines for Responsible Use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) at USF.

units.why: "All technology and technology services must undergo a data privacy, security and technical evaluation as part of the New Technology Assessment process" is an institutional review requirement before tools are adopted. That is P65.
units.anchor: All technology and technology services must undergo a data privacy, security and technical evaluation

units.why: The matrix footnote says data above the permitted level "must only be entered into GenAI tools that have been assessed and explicitly approved for such use by the CIO". It limits what data go into which tools, which is P50 (protect data, prefer vetted tools).
units.anchor: only be entered into GenAI tools that have been assessed and explicitly approved
units.frag_end: approved for such use by the CIO.

units.why: "Be mindful of FERPA and HIPAA-protected data" asks users to take care with protected data in GenAI tools. That is P50, as a softer instruction.
units.anchor: Be mindful of
units.policy: Users are mindful of FERPA and HIPAA-protected data when using GenAI tools.

units.why: The application matrix lists categories of GenAI applications with the "Highest Level Data Classification Allowed" for each, for example Enterprise Administered Applications that "have undergone the New Technology Assessment process and are administered by USF". It names approved tool types and their data limits, which is P92 (use approved tools).
units.anchor: Applications that have undergone the New Technology Assessment process and are administered by USF.
units.fit_note: The matrix also sorts publicly available chatbots and administrative tools by the data classification they may receive, which P92 does not capture.

units.why: "DLI offers a variety of classes to help faculty and staff develop their skills in GenAI" is training offered to employees. P63 (support faculty in learning AI) fits, although it covers staff as well.
units.anchor: DLI offers a variety of classes to help faculty and staff develop their skills
units.fit_note: The training is for faculty and staff, not faculty only.

units.why: "GenAI tools can support student learning in various ways" names a benefit of AI for learning without setting a rule. That is P87.
units.anchor: GenAI tools can support student learning in various ways.

units.why: "Consult with an expert on incorporating or restricting GenAI in your course" offers instructors consultations before setting course AI rules. P63 fits.
units.anchor: Consult with an expert on incorporating or restricting GenAI in your course.

units.why: "Select a customizable syllabus statement to fit your course" directs instructors to the university's template statements. P110 fits because the institution supplies templates for adoption.
units.anchor: Select a customizable
units.policy: Instructors select a customizable syllabus statement to fit their course.

units.why: "Resources to share with your students and include in your syllabus" supplies materials for students and asks instructors to pass them on. P115 (point to further resources) fits.
units.anchor: to share with your students and include in your syllabus.

notes: The Guidelines for Responsible Use of AI at USF (usf.service-now.com KB15409) could not be fetched, so its content is not coded. Only two university-layer documents were coded; no computing, school or course documents were included. The syllabus page is a menu of templates, so its three options are coded as units under a delegates stance, with the third option's note to instructors (unenforceability, equity, embedded AI) coded as separate units.
